evidence.methodology_note: Frozen rubric defined below before scoring. Same rubric structure is intended to apply unchanged to all 10 languages; this shard scores only the assigned language (Swift). Snapshot date: 2026-09-22. Sources: swift.org official install/release pages, swiftlang GitHub orgs, and independent technical commentary, retrieved via web search on 2026-09-22.

metric.installation_distribution_experie.adjustment_note: Score rounded down 2 points from raw rubric sum to reflect that Swift's package/distribution story is fragmented across three unofficial, competing third-party package registries (no single de-facto standard), noted as declared context evidence and not double-counted against Package/Dependency Management Quality.
metric.installation_distribution_experie.contextual_caveat: There is no de-facto standard for a package registry related to Swift packages.

observations.citation: Linux macOS Windows · Select Linux platform: Amazon Linux Debian Fedora Red Hat Ubuntu
observations.note: swift.org publishes dedicated official install pages for macOS, Linux (Amazon Linux, Debian, Fedora, Red Hat, and multiple Ubuntu versions), and Windows.

observations.citation: Once swiftly is installed it will automatically install the latest released toolchain.
observations.note: Swiftly is the official first-party toolchain installer and version manager for macOS and Linux; Windows uses a winget package id instead of Swiftly.

observations.citation: Docker Official Image packaging for Swift.
observations.note: Swift maintains an official Docker Hub image plus a container-publishing plugin for Swift Package Manager.
Linux tarball/SDK downloads on swift.org ship alongside a PGP signature link for verification.

observations.citation: 1 Swift toolchain is provided by Saleem Abdulrasool.
observations.note: Per-platform pages give copy-paste install commands, editor/LSP setup, and a first-run tutorial, but Windows support is comparatively newer and historically maintained by a single named contributor rather than a broad team.
Formats include macOS .pkg, Linux tarball/RPM/Docker/Swiftly, Windows winget/manual installer, and IDE-bundled distribution via Xcode.

A_official_installers_three_os_families.desc: First-party installers/binaries for Windows, macOS, Linux from the language's canonical distribution channel.

B_native_pkg_or_version_manager_integrat.desc: First-party package-manager entries (winget/apt/dnf) or an official version-manager tool comparable to rustup/nvm.

C_container_cloud_distribution.desc: Official container images maintained by the language org.

D_download_verification.desc: Checksums/PGP signatures published for release artifacts.

E_install_doc_clarity.desc: Completeness/clarity of official per-platform install documentation.

F_artifact_format_breadth.desc: Breadth of installable artifact formats (tarball, pkg/installer, IDE-bundled, SDK images).

metric.toolchain_stability_release_matur.adjustment_note: Score adjusted down 5 points from the raw rubric sum because ABI stability was historically declared only for Apple platforms first, with non-Apple platforms (Linux, Windows) treated as maturing separately for a period, a caveat retained as evidence though largely resolved by later unification work.
metric.toolchain_stability_release_matur.contextual_caveat: On non-Apple platforms (such as Linux) the ABI is not yet fully stable in order to allow for more vetting.

observations.citation: Swift 5 provides binary compatibility for apps: a guarantee that going forward, an app built with one version of the Swift compiler will be able to talk to a library built with another version.
observations.note: Swift 5 introduced a documented ABI stability guarantee that an app built with one compiler version can talk to a library built with another.

observations.citation: Source compatibility with Swift 3.0 is a top priority.
observations.note: Every major/minor release since Swift 3.1 has shipped an official release-process post declaring source compatibility as a top priority, with narrowly scoped, documented exceptions for compiler bug fixes.

observations.citation: Three specialized workgroups govern evolution in their respective domains: Language Steering Group (language/stdlib), Ecosystem Steering Group (package manager), and Testing Workgroup (Swift Testing).
observations.note: Swift Evolution is a formal, governed proposal process with dedicated steering/workgroups tracking every release from version 2.2 through 6.2+, each beginning with a public forum announcement and ending in a release blog post.

observations.citation: You can see from the support page's chart that every version of the Swift 6 compiler as of Xcode 26 still supports the Swift 4 language mode
observations.note: Swift maintains explicit language-compatibility modes (e.g., Swift 4, 4.2, 5, 6) so older code continues to compile under newer compilers, with upcoming-feature flags for gradual adoption.

observations.citation: Swift 6.4 unifies building across Linux, macOS, Windows
observations.note: Releases have shipped on a roughly annual-to-biannual cadence from Swift 3 (2016) through Swift 6.x releases in 2024-2026, including a 6.4 release unifying the cross-platform build experience.

observations.citation: Swift snapshots are prebuilt binaries that are automatically created from the branch.
observations.note: Development snapshots are automatically built from branches and CI-tested, but are explicitly distinguished from official releases which undergo fuller testing.

A_abi_stability_guarantee.desc: Documented, frozen ABI/binary-compatibility guarantee across compiler versions.

B_source_compatibility_commitment.desc: Explicit, repeatedly honored source-compatibility policy across releases.

C_transparent_release_process.desc: Published, predictable release-process documentation and governance for each version.

D_versioned_compat_mechanism.desc: Opt-in language-mode mechanism letting old code keep compiling under newer compilers.

E_sustained_cadence.desc: Regular release cadence sustained over many years.

F_prerelease_pipeline.desc: CI-tested snapshot/pre-release channel clearly separated from vetted stable releases.
